title: Users see stale data after a successful update
description: Problem: Users see stale data after a successful update. Solve this problem with multiple approaches and detailed explanations.

data.text: A user edits a record, sees the success message, and refreshes the page. The change is there. But if they stay on the list page, the updated row still shows the old values until they force a hard refresh. In a single-page application this means the local cache or client state is not being invalidated after the mutation.

items: The list is cached by React Query, SWR, or a custom hook and never invalidated after the mutation.
The mutation updates the server but does not update the local cache or global store.
Optimistic updates were rolled back silently because the server returned a non-200 status.
Multiple queries cache the same data under different keys, so invalidating one key leaves others stale.
Server responses are cached by a service worker or CDN without revalidation headers.
The UI reads from a stale closure or module-level variable instead of the current query result.

terms.definition: The process of marking cached data as outdated so the next read fetches fresh data.
Updating the UI before the server confirms the mutation, then rolling back if the request fails.
A caching strategy that serves cached data immediately while updating it in the background.
An identifier used by data-fetching libraries to track and cache requests.

data.text: Inspect the network tab and the data-fetching library's devtools. If the list request is not refetched after the mutation, the cache entry is still valid according to the library. If the mutation returns 200 but the list does not update, the problem is cache invalidation or optimistic update logic.

data.title: Invalidate the broadest query that covers the stale data
data.text: If the list and the detail view use different keys, invalidating only the detail key will not refresh the list. Invalidate the shared parent query or use dependent queries so they update together.

data.caption: Data flow after a successful mutation
data.definition:
graph TD
    A[User edits record] --> B[Send mutation to server]
    B --> C{Server responds 200?}
    C -->|Yes| D[Update local cache or invalidate]
    C -->|No| E[Rollback optimistic update]
    D --> F{Strategy}
    F -->|Invalidate| G[Mark query stale]
    F -->|Optimistic| H[Write new value to cache immediately]
    G --> I[List refetches from server]
    H --> J[List shows new value immediately]
    I --> K[List confirms server state]
    J --> K
    E --> L[Show error and restore previous value]
    K --> M[UI stays in sync]
    L --> N[User retries or cancels]

items.question: Why does a hard refresh fix the stale data?
items.answer: A hard refresh bypasses the client-side cache and fetches fresh HTML and data from the server. The fact that it fixes the issue proves the server has the correct data and the problem is local caching.

items.question: Should I use optimistic updates everywhere?
items.answer: No. Optimistic updates are best for fast, low-risk mutations like liking a post or toggling a setting. For financial or irreversible actions, wait for the server confirmation and show a loading state.

items.question: How do I debug which query is stale?
items.answer: Use the React Query or SWR devtools. Inspect the cache entries for the affected resource and check their status, data, and updatedAt timestamps. Look for entries that were created before the mutation.

data.title: Fix stale data after a mutation
data.description: Add cache invalidation or optimistic updates to a mutation in a real app.
steps: Find a mutation in your app that updates data shown in a list.
Confirm the list becomes stale after the mutation completes.
Add cache invalidation for the list query after the mutation succeeds.
Optional: replace invalidation with an optimistic update and handle rollback.
Verify the list updates immediately and stays in sync after a manual refetch.
data.expectedOutcome: The list should show the updated value immediately, and a manual refetch should confirm the server and client agree.

data.title: Summary
points: Stale data after a mutation is a cache invalidation problem, not a server problem.
Use library devtools to inspect cache status and timestamps.
Invalidate parent queries when child data changes.
Optimistic updates improve perceived speed but require careful rollback logic.
Always verify the server response before declaring the UI consistent
data.takeaway: Users trust what they see on the screen. If the UI shows old data after a successful action, the application feels broken regardless of what the server actually stored.
